title: 06 — Voice Assistants
html:
06 — Voice Assistants

The one idea: a voice assistant is a chatbot with two hard extra problems: hearing and speaking fast enough to feel natural, and knowing when the person has finished talking. Most of the engineering is latency and turn-taking, not the language model.

1. What it is

Two architectures:

Architecture Flow Strengths Weaknesses
Cascaded pipeline Audio → VAD (voice activity detection) → STT (speech-to-text) → LLM → TTS (text-to-speech) → audio Choose the best part for each stage. Full transcripts for logging and evaluation. Works with any LLM and your tools More stages add latency, so you must stream every stage
Speech-to-speech (realtime) Audio in, audio out from one model Lowest latency, keeps tone and emotion Fewer model choices, harder to inspect and control, cost per audio token

Building blocks, checked 2026-10-27 (from vendor and comparison sources, so confirm current models and prices):

Stage Options
Orchestration and real-time transport LiveKit Agents (WebRTC, SIP telephony), Pipecat (Python frame pipeline), managed platforms (Vapi, Retell)
STT Deepgram (Nova models, with an end-of-turn model), Azure AI Speech, AssemblyAI, open-source Whisper (self-hosted)
TTS ElevenLabs (voice quality and cloning), Cartesia, Azure AI Speech neural voices, Deepgram Aura
Speech-to-speech OpenAI Realtime models, Azure Voice Live API, other providers' live APIs
Turn detection VAD (for example Silero), plus semantic end-of-turn models (LiveKit's turn detector, Pipecat's Smart Turn)
Telephony SIP trunks (Twilio, Telnyx), or the platforms' built-in phone numbers

2. Why it matters

  • People notice delays above roughly a second, and interruptions that cut them off.
  • Phone audio is narrowband and noisy, so STT accuracy on account numbers and names needs testing.
  • Voice data is personal data: consent, retention and redaction apply (OL 17).

3. The main ideas

3.1 The cascaded pipeline

---
title: Cascaded voice agent — every stage streams
---
flowchart LR
    MIC["Caller audio<br/>(WebRTC or SIP)"] --> VAD["VAD + end-of-turn model"]
    VAD --> STT["Streaming STT<br/>(partial and final text)"]
    STT --> LLM["LLM with tools<br/>(streams tokens)"]
    LLM --> TTS["Streaming TTS<br/>(starts on the first sentence)"]
    TTS --> SPK["Audio back to caller"]
    MIC -. "caller speaks again" .-> BI["Barge-in: stop TTS,<br/>cancel LLM, listen"]
    BI --> STT

3.2 Latency budget

Sum the stages to "time to first audio". Comparison guides quote roughly 450 to 600 ms end to end for premium cascaded stacks, and under about 500 ms voice-to-voice for speech-to-speech models. Treat these as targets to measure, not guarantees.

Ways to cut it:

  • Stream everything. Start TTS on the first sentence, not the full reply.
  • Keep the model's first reply short. Use a smaller, faster model for voice turns.
  • Run in a region near the callers.
  • Use a semantic end-of-turn model, so you don't need long silence thresholds.

3.3 Turn-taking and barge-in

  • End of turn: silence alone is a poor signal. People pause mid-sentence. Combine VAD timing with a semantic end-of-turn model.
  • Barge-in: when the caller starts talking during the reply, stop TTS, cancel the in-flight LLM response, and listen.
  • Backchannels: "uh-huh" shouldn't count as an interruption. Tune it.

3.4 Designing for the ear

  • Short sentences. One question at a time. Read numbers back to confirm them ("that's 4, 2, 7, 1, correct?").
  • No markdown or lists in voice replies. Instruct the model to write speech.
  • Clear handoff to a human ("I'll transfer you now"), and a way to repeat.

4. Working code

The script detects speech frames by energy in a synthetic signal, applies two silence thresholds for end of turn, and sums a latency budget. numpy only. Production systems use trained VAD and turn models, but the frame-by-frame idea is the same.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
SR = 16_000                                       # 16 kHz mono: the usual input for speech-to-text
def tone(seconds, freq=220.0, amp=0.3):            # a stand-in for speech
    t = np.arange(int(seconds * SR)) / SR
    return amp * np.sin(2 * np.pi * freq * t) * (1 + 0.3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 3 * t))
silence = lambda s: rng.normal(0, 0.01, int(s * SR))  # background noise
audio = np.concatenate([silence(0.5), tone(1.2), silence(0.25), tone(0.6), silence(1.0)])

# 1. Voice activity detection (VAD) by frame energy. Production systems use trained VAD models
#    (and semantic end-of-turn models), but the frame-by-frame idea is the same.
FRAME = int(0.02 * SR)                            # 20 ms frames
energy = np.array([np.sqrt(np.mean(audio[i:i + FRAME] ** 2)) for i in range(0, len(audio) - FRAME, FRAME)])
speech = energy > 0.05

# 2. End of turn: the user has stopped only after enough continuous silence. Too short a wait
#    cuts people off mid-sentence; too long feels sluggish.
def end_of_turn(speech, hangover_ms):
    need, quiet, heard = hangover_ms // 20, 0, False
    for i, s in enumerate(speech):
        heard |= s
        quiet = 0 if s else quiet + 1
        if heard and quiet >= need:
            return (i + 1) * 20
    return None
for hang in (200, 500):
    print(f"silence threshold {hang} ms -> turn ends at {end_of_turn(speech, hang)} ms")
print("speech runs (ms):", [(int(a) * 20, int(b) * 20) for a, b in
      zip(np.flatnonzero(np.diff(np.r_[0, speech.astype(int)]) == 1),
          np.flatnonzero(np.diff(np.r_[speech.astype(int), 0]) == -1) + 1)])

# 3. A latency budget for a cascaded voice agent (illustrative numbers, per stage).
budget = {"end-of-turn wait": 500, "speech-to-text final": 200, "model first token": 450,
          "text-to-speech first audio": 150, "network": 100}
print("time to first audio:", sum(budget.values()), "ms", budget)

Output:

silence threshold 200 ms -> turn ends at 1900 ms
silence threshold 500 ms -> turn ends at 3060 ms
speech runs (ms): [(500, 1700), (1940, 2560)]
time to first audio: 1400 ms {'end-of-turn wait': 500, 'speech-to-text final': 200, 'model first token': 450, 'text-to-speech first audio': 150, 'network': 100}

What to notice:

  • The speaker pauses for 240 ms between two phrases (speech runs end at 1700 ms and restart at 1940 ms). A 200 ms silence threshold ends the turn at 1900 ms, which cuts them off. A 500 ms threshold waits for the real end (3060 ms), but adds latency. That trade-off is why semantic end-of-turn models exist.
  • Time to first audio is 1,400 ms in this illustrative budget, and the end-of-turn wait is the largest single item.

A LiveKit or Pipecat agent wires real STT, LLM and TTS services into exactly these stages. Check each framework's current quick start, because their APIs change often (one 2026 guide notes that LiveKit samples on PyPI lagged its docs).

5. Common mistakes

  1. Not streaming. Waiting for full STT, then a full LLM reply, then full TTS, feels like seconds of dead air.
  2. Silence-only end of turn. It cuts people off, or feels sluggish.
  3. Markdown in spoken replies. TTS reads "asterisk asterisk".
  4. No barge-in. Callers can't correct the assistant.
  5. Recording without consent or retention rules.

6. Exercise (2 hours)

  1. Change the pause in the script to 400 ms, and find the threshold that neither cuts off nor waits longer than 600 ms.
  2. Add barge-in: if speech starts while a (made-up) TTS playback is running, stop playback and log the time.
  3. Build a hello-world voice agent with LiveKit Agents or Pipecat using their quick start, and measure time to first audio.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What are the stages of a cascaded voice pipeline?
  2. Why is silence alone a poor end-of-turn signal?
  3. What does barge-in require the system to do?
  4. When would you pick speech-to-speech over a cascaded pipeline?
  5. Name three ways to cut time to first audio.

Answers

  1. VAD and turn detection, streaming STT, the LLM, then streaming TTS, over a real-time transport.
  2. People pause mid-sentence. A short threshold cuts them off, and a long one adds delay.
  3. Stop TTS playback, cancel the in-flight model response, and resume listening.
  4. When the lowest latency and natural tone matter most, and you can accept less control and inspection.
  5. Stream every stage, keep first replies short (and use a faster model), and use a semantic end-of-turn model and a nearby region.

8. Sources
